races.title: State House, District 76
races.note: The top two finishers from the Nov 3, 2026 count. Everyone else in this race is coming.

cands.name: Greg Edds
cands.bio: State Farm insurance agent in Salisbury for about 30 years, with the CLU and ChFC designations. Rowan County Commissioner and board chairman, 2014-2026, the longest-serving chairman in county history. Past chair of the Rowan County Republican Party. Won the NC House District 76 seat in 2026.

controversies.text: As Rowan County board chair, Edds drew scrutiny over the board's 2024 zoning change that allowed data centers at the Long Ferry Road site. In April 2026 the board voted unanimously for a one-year moratorium on new data centers. It excludes the Long Ferry project under state law. Edds said getting a citizen group involved sooner would have helped.

cands.gaps: His birthplace and where he grew up could not be found. No documented personal votes or statements on data centers, property taxes, land ownership by investors or foreigners, growth limits, immigration, policing, guns, abortion or school choice were found. The data center controversy is described only briefly in a Wikipedia summary, with no detail on his role or response. His campaign site speaks generally of "industrial recruitment projects" and "smart, sustainable" economic development, without naming specific projects or policies. Ballotpedia lists no endorsements for him, and he did not complete its candidate survey.

local.label: Roots 55: He moved to Salisbury as an adult in 1995, about 31 years ago, and has lived in Rowan County since, where he raised three children; his birthplace and upbringing aren't documented in these sources.

score.why: Raised $0, under $5,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

qual.background: Ran a State Farm agency in Salisbury for about 30 years after about 10 years in State Farm corporate roles, and served as Rowan County Commissioner and board chairman from 2014 to 2026, with county budgeting and zoning in the role. He has no prior state legislative service.
qual.why: He has 12 years in local elected office, including leading a county board that handles budgets and zoning, plus a long career as a business owner. That fits the middle range; he has no state legislative or chamber leadership experience.

cands.name: Scott Huffman
cands.bio: Navy veteran (petty officer 2nd class) and small business owner in information technology and cybersecurity. Founded Indivisible Charlotte and served on the Mecklenburg County Democratic Party board. Ran for U.S. House in 2018 (lost primary), 2020 and 2022 (lost general). No elected office held.
cands.gaps: We found no record of any elected or legislative office, so there are no official actions to report. We could not find when he moved away from or back to North Carolina after his Navy service. His campaign site does not address homestead property taxes, limits on out-of-state or institutional land buyers, or growth and development limits beyond data centers. It does not address police pay or pensions or abortion restrictions beyond a general stance. He did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey. No news reporting on controversies was available.

local.label: Roots 100: Ballotpedia says he was born in Salisbury, NC, and graduated from North Rowan High School in 1980. His 2021 candidate survey says he was raised in Spencer, NC.

score.why: Raised $0, under $5,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

qual.background: Started an IT business and grew it to over 3,000 customers. Served in the U.S. Navy for more than seven years, including work for the Joint Chiefs and at the Naval Communications Center. Has held no elected or legislative office.
qual.why: Business ownership puts him in the middle range. He has no legislative, policy-staff or budget career and has never held office; his three congressional runs were all losses.

land_positions.quote_or_summary: Campaign website says "No data center gets built here without strict rules that protect our water, our power bills, and our neighborhoods." It argues unregulated AI data centers strain the grid and raise bills. This calls for strict rules, not a ban.
